A strawman argument is a typically shallow, showy, and good sounding argument that misrepresents somehow the core of the discussion. Not always used intentionally or maliciously, strawmen are a way to control the direction of discussion. If someone disproves a strawman, they have only disproven one of many weak arguments their opponent can keep making up and throwing at them, keeping the discussion to topics of the opponent's choosing.

Some strawman examples are found in arguments that (for example) declining religiosity equals declining morality. It can be supported with emotional appeals to subjective experience, and by the fact that religions are well known for their moral guidelines. Authoritarians can point out that there is no unifying moral code for people to follow outside of religion. Citing famously atheistic "bad people" is another common tactic.

A more in depth ponder of the argument comes up with reasons why the arguments are irrelevant. Hedonism is well documented in history which shows that subjective experience of modern depravity is no evidence for a recent decline. Religions do have moral guidelines but a rational thinker can see many examples of religious guidelines that are ignored, or amended, or reinterpreted to suit the current culture, showing that while religion may command a certain moral code it is ultimately the people who define their own moral code. The authoritarian argument distracts from realizing that there are good and bad people in every group, everywhere, in all of time, and that it is impossible to know what principles drove historical figures even if they were outwardly devout. A closer inspection of historical figures would show little correlation if any on the simplistic premise of religious person=moral, areligious person=amoral.

If Phaedrus hadn't been so excited over the arrival of the new 'reservoir' elements, he would have probably thought this experiment through a little more.

At the very least, he would have placed a sign or barricade in the hallway, or maybe he could have even opened the door to check for passerby.

As it were, Phaedrus had been so focused on getting this prototype functioning that he neglected the most basic considerations for safety, and somehow forgot that the walls were paper thin. So it should have been to nobody's surprise other than his own that when he activated the new force array, something unexpected would happen. In this case, it cracked one wall, and sent the device hurtling through another wall.

It also happened that as the device was hurled out, the Illithid were right about to reach the door. The sudden appearance of a metallic box smashing through the wall, accompanied by roughly an entire minute of unprintable obscenities, was mildly startling to say the least.

After roughly a minute of stunned silence, the door opened, and Phaedrus, looking slightly more disheveled than usual, spoke.

"You know, you could have knocked."

*****

"As I was saying, they should really reassign the person who came up with the building codes for these laboratories, I mean their decision making is so questionable. Their reasoning for thin walls was 'Due to the heightened risk of destruction of laboratory spaces, these spaces should be constructed as cheaply as possible to minimize replacement costs.' No thought as to actually, you know, making walls that could stand up after these accidents."

Phaedrus, seated comfortably behind his desk, had been discussing building codes, amongst other things, for the past 20 minutes. A visible air of boredom emanated from his audience, but Phaedrus didn't seem to notice, or even more likely simply did not care.

"Yes. and chop off the head of the designer I presume?" Trovita replied curtly as always. Phaedrus' antics were humourous, but such a divergence at a critical moment was irksome.

"Alright, I'll stop. So, why did you bring these guests here?"

"We've discussed this already Phaedrus, I believe their work will be of interest to you, as your work would be of interest to them." came the reply.

"I've taken a look at their circuitry, it has very simularities to what we are doing, but whatever they are trying to achieve is rather different from what exactly we are trying to achieve. I do see how we could make this work. What do you think, yeah you, the one who looks slightly more purple than the others."

Greethus seemed both vexed and insulted by this rather inept description. His skin was a delicable shade of blueberry blue, not 'purple', he had half a mind to return a barrage of insults, but barely managed to restrain himself in the interest of preserving workable relations between species.

"Yes, some sort of agreement would be greatly appreciated. We look forwards to the progress this may lead to in both our fields."

Phaedrus showed some mild satisfaction. "Wonderful, now all we have to do is get you some accomodations and a workspace, preferably in the same building. Might have to requisition some supplies and rations, you know, the usual."

Phaedrus took out a massive stack of forms and paperwork.

"Just fill this out by tomorrow morning, or don't, I really don't care. We'll get you guys set up temporarily in the meantime. Welcome to Sentenza, Illithid. I hope you enjoy your stay."

Phaedrus, while experimenting with force circuits, breaks a laboratory wall. He also startles a bunch of Illithid on the other side of said wall. After a short meeting, and a showing of a complete lack of social aptitude from Phaedrus' behalf, the an agreement is worked out and a stack of paperwork produced for the Illithid.
